article.title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
article.subtitle: This scenario is not very likely — but probably worth a bet at 300:1

extraction.summary: Silver responds to Nate Cohn's NYT argument that Harris's Electoral College penalty will be smaller in 2024. He agrees the gap is narrower than in 2016 and 2020 but says it is larger than the Times estimates: 1.3 points in Silver Bulletin polling averages and 1.5 points in the forecast, versus 0.7 for the Times. Along the way he explains several model mechanics: the regression blend and its weight, the fundamentals prior, the bottom-up popular vote built from 56 contests, imputation for unpolled states, and 40,000 simulations. He dissects the 102 simulations in which Harris wins the Electoral College but loses the popular vote and finds they mostly run through a MI+PA+WI+NE2 path. He closes by noting that swing-state ground game and ad effects, which the simulations don't model, could make a Democrat-favoring split more likely than the model's ~300:1.

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model runs 40,000 simulations per forecast update.
findings.evidence_quote: we ended up with 102 simulations (out of 40,000) in which Harris did win the Electoral College but lost the popular vote

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model's national popular vote forecast is not based directly on national polls. It is the sum of projected results in 56 contests: 50 states, DC, Nebraska's three congressional districts and Maine's two. National polls play only an indirect role, such as helping infer results in sparsely polled states.

quantities.name: contests projected
quantities.context: 50 states + DC + 3 NE CDs + 2 ME CDs

findings.rationale: This bottom-up method is sometimes more accurate than national polls alone.
findings.evidence_quote: our popular vote forecast isn’t actually based on national polls. Rather, it’s based on summing up the results from the 56 contests the model projects

findings.statement: In 2012, Silver's bottom-up (sum of states) popular vote method correctly showed Obama winning the popular vote by a wider margin than national polls projected.
findings.rationale: Cited as evidence supporting the bottom-up approach.
findings.evidence_quote: like in 2012 when it correctly had Barack Obama winning the popular vote by a wider margin than national polls projected

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast differs from its polling average in two ways. It incorporates a 'fundamentals' prior based on the economy and incumbency. It also blends the polling average with a regression that infers each state's result from national polls and polls of other states.
findings.evidence_quote: incorporating a “fundamentals” prior based on the economy and incumbency, and blending our polling averages with a regression analysis that makes inferences about the race from national polls and polls of other states

findings.statement: The fundamentals prior and the regression component get less weight as Election Day approaches. By Election Day the model defaults toward being more 'polls-only'.
findings.evidence_quote: Those factors play less and less of a role as the model defaults toward being more “polls-only” by Election Day

findings.statement: The weight on the state polling average versus the regression depends on how much recent polling a state has. With heavy recent polling in Pennsylvania, 93% of the weight went to the polling average and 7% to the regression.
findings.rationale: More recent state polling means more trust in the state's own average.
findings.evidence_quote: with a lot of recent polling in Pennsylvania, 93 percent of the weight goes to the polling average and just 7 percent to the regression

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin Pennsylvania forecast table lists 10 steps from polling average to win probability: (1) polling average; (2) adjust for bounces and recent events; (3) adjusted polling average; (4) reallocate undecided and third-party votes; (5) reallocated vote share; (6) blend with regression; (7) snapshot; (8) blend with economic fundamentals; (9) projected vote share; (10) chance of winning.

In the Sept 26 Pennsylvania forecast table, the inputs and outputs were as follows. The polling average was Harris 48.8 / Trump 47.3, and the bounce adjustment was about zero. Reallocating undecided and third-party votes added +1.6 to each candidate (50.4 / 48.9). The regression estimate was 49.6 / 49.7, blended at weight 0.06. The snapshot was 50.3 / 48.9. The economic fundamentals estimate was 48.9 / 50.3, blended at weight 0.14. The final projection was 50.1 / 49.1, with a Harris win probability of 59.1%.

quantities.name: fundamentals blend weight
quantities.context: PA, Sept 26 2024, roughly 6 weeks before election

quantities.name: undecided/third-party reallocation
quantities.context: PA, applied equally to both candidates

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast reallocates undecided and third-party votes to the major candidates. In Pennsylvania on Sept 26 the reallocation was equal, +1.6 points each.

For states with no polling, such as New Jersey and Illinois in 2024, the model imputes results using information from other polls. Those imputations showed Harris's margins in the bluest states down from Biden's 2020 numbers, enough to reduce but not erase the Electoral College gap.
findings.rationale: Silver says the imputations are usually pretty reasonable.
findings.evidence_quote: Whether through imputation or by directly looking at the polling, the model does expect Harris’s margins in some of the bluest states to be down from Biden’s numbers

findings.statement: In 2024 the most populous blue states without any polls were New Jersey and Illinois. Unlike some past years, no pollster had yet run a 50-state survey, so the model relied on imputation for these states.
findings.evidence_quote: usually, some brave pollster has conducted a 50-state survey by now

findings.statement: The Silver Bulletin polling average table shows only contests surveyed by at least three distinct pollsters or with at least five polls.
In the model, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are correlated but not perfectly, so winning all three is a 'correlated parlay' that remains hard to hit.
findings.rationale: State-specific shocks, such as a Wisconsin polling error or Arab American voters in Michigan swinging on Gaza, can flip a single state.
findings.evidence_quote: Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are correlated, but not perfectly so, and as any sports bettor will tell you, correlated parlays are still hard to win

findings.statement: Of the 102 simulations in which Harris won the Electoral College but lost the popular vote, Harris won MI in 90%, PA in 88%, WI in 81% and NE-2 in 82%. She won NC in 31%, GA in 21% and AZ in 3%, averaging 277 electoral votes. A few of these were extreme-tail outcomes.
findings.evidence_quote: Harris won Michigan in 90 percent of these simulations

findings.statement: On Sept 26, 2024 the model gave a 20% chance that Harris wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College, versus 0.3% for the reverse split. Harris was a 3:1 favorite in the popular vote while the Electoral College was roughly a toss-up.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s a 20 percent chance that Harris wins the popular but loses the Electoral College, but only a 0.3 percent chance of the same thing happening to Donald Trump

findings.statement: The model projected Harris +2.5 nationally and +1.0 in Pennsylvania (the tipping point), a point-estimate Electoral College gap of 1.5 points. Averaged across simulations, the gap is about 2 points. Splits can occur at popular vote margins anywhere from about Trump +1 to Harris +5.

quantities.name: average simulated EC gap
quantities.context: after uncertainty; about half the 2020 gap

findings.rationale: Because outcomes are probabilistic, small misses in PA, MI or WI widen the effective gap.
findings.evidence_quote: in our average simulation after accounting for this uncertainty, the Electoral College / popular vote winds up being about 2 points, not 1.5

findings.statement: The model's conditional win probability by popular vote bin shows the Electoral College bias. Harris's win probability is 10.5% at D+0 to +1, 32.8% at D+1 to +2, 63.3% at D+2 to +3, 87.0% at D+3 to +4, 96.7% at D+4 to +5 and 99.5% at D+5 to +6. Trump wins 96.9% of the time at R+0 to +1, and Harris wins only 3.0% there. Harris's mean electoral votes are 274.0 at D+2 to +3 and 243.4 at D+0 to +1.
Some simulations produce no Electoral College majority for either candidate (e.g., 269-269 ties), so win probabilities do not always sum to 100%.

Silver Bulletin polling averages on Sept 26, 2024 had the following margins: National D+2.8 (49.0-46.2), PA D+1.5, MI D+2.3, WI D+2.2, NC R+0.5, GA R+1, AZ R+1, FL R+3.4, NV D+1.1, MN D+5.9, NM D+8.1, TX R+5.6. Polling averages and the forecast differ.
findings.evidence_quote: In our averages, Harris leads by 2.8 points nationally but by 1.5 points in Pennsylvania.

findings.statement: The regression component estimated Pennsylvania as roughly a tie based on polls of other states, versus Harris +1.5 in the PA polling average.
findings.evidence_quote: the regression analysis thinks that the state “should” be a tie based on the polling it sees of other states instead of Harris +1.5

findings.statement: Polling averages contain more noise than people assume, and a state's recent gains, such as Harris's post-debate gains in PA, may revert to the mean.
findings.evidence_quote: there could be some reversion to the mean and there’s more noise in polling averages than people might assume

findings.statement: The simulations do not model swing-state-specific effects, such as a Harris overperformance in swing states from ground game or heavier ad spending. They also do not model countervailing pro-Trump swing-state effects, such as RFK Jr. telling his voters to back Trump only in swing states.

quantities.name: model odds of Harris EC win / PV loss

findings.rationale: These factors are usually minor, but even a few tenths of a point in swing states could make a Democrat-favoring split somewhat more likely.
findings.evidence_quote: There’s one other factor our simulations don’t really consider

findings.statement: Silver stresses that the model is probabilistic, not deterministic. Point estimates such as a 1.5-point Electoral College gap will be wrong, and the distribution of outcomes is what matters.
findings.evidence_quote: our model is probabilistic, not deterministic

findings.statement: The forecast has an 'adjust for bounces & recent events' step applied to the polling average. It was about 0 in PA on Sept 26.

NYT (Nate Cohn) polling averages put the 2024 Electoral College gap at 0.7 points: D+2.6 national versus D+1.8 in the tipping point, PA. Silver Bulletin's averages give 1.3 points and its forecast gives 1.5.
findings.evidence_quote: the gap is only 0.7 points instead, according to the Times’s polling averages

political_insights.insight: The Electoral College penalty for Democrats was nearly 3 points in 2016 (PA tipping point) and nearly 4 points in 2020 (WI tipping point), and appears smaller in 2024.
political_insights.evidence: 2016 D+2.1 national vs R+0.8 tipping point; 2020 D+4.5 vs D+0.6.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Don't assume a fixed Electoral College bias; let the state polls determine it.

political_insights.insight: In 2020 Pennsylvania leaned GOP relative to the nation by about 3 points: Biden won PA by 1.2 and the nation by 4.5. A repeat gap would mean Harris losing PA by roughly 50,000 votes.
Democratic deterioration in deep-blue states like New York shaves wasted votes and reduces the Electoral College gap without costing Democrats those states.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Bottom-up state modeling captures the effect of wasted votes on the popular vote/EC gap.

political_insights.insight: In 2022 polls were not systematically biased against Democrats overall, but Democrats tended to slightly beat their polls in the closest state and district contests.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Possible swing-state turnout effects not captured by the model.

political_insights.insight: Democrats have won the popular vote by at least 1.5 points in each of the past four elections.
Arab American voters in Michigan swinging toward Trump over Gaza is a state-specific risk to Harris.

references.description: Nate Cohn NYT article arguing the Electoral College penalty is smaller in 2024
Silver Bulletin model methodology ('takes some additional steps')
Silver Bulletin June 2024 Biden-version forecast launch discussing the MI+PA+WI path
Article on noise in polling averages
Article on 2022 polls not being biased against Democrats

open_questions: Functional form of the regression model that infers state results from national and other-state polls.
How the regression weight is determined as a function of the amount and recency of state polling.
How undecided and third-party votes are reallocated (equal split vs. proportional).
Construction of the economic and incumbency fundamentals prior and its weight schedule over time.
What the 'snapshot' step represents and how it differs from the blended vote share.
The correlation structure across states (e.g., MI/PA/WI correlation parameters).
How states without polls (NJ, IL) are imputed.
